Domestic Violence is any act against a person, particularly women, which results in misery or suffering physically, sexually, psychologically, and/or domestic neglect including threats to commit acts, coercion, or unlawful deprivation of liberty within the household. 5. Elimination of Domestic Violence is a guarantee provided by the state to prevent the occurrence of domestic violence, prosecute perpetrators of domestic violence, and protect victims of domestic violence. 6. Trafficking in Persons is the act of recruitment, transportation, harboring, transfer, relocation, or receipt of a person by means of threat of violence, use of violence, abduction, confinement, fraud, deception, abuse of power or position of vulnerability, debt bondage or giving payments or benefits, so as to obtain the consent of a person having control over another person, whether conducted within a country or between countries, for the purpose of exploitation or resulting in a person being exploited. 7. Victim of Trafficking in Persons is a person who experiences psychological, mental, physical, sexual, economic, and/or social suffering, resulting from the crime of trafficking in persons. 8. Violence is any act that results in or can result in misery or suffering whether physical, sexual, economic, psychological to the victim. 9. Physical violence is any act that causes pain, injury, wounds, or disability to a person's body, miscarriage, unconsciousness and/or causes death. 10. Psychological violence is an act that causes fear, loss of self-confidence, loss of ability to act, feeling of helplessness and/or severe psychological suffering to a person. 11. Sexual violence is an act in the form of sexual harassment, forced sexual intercourse, forced sexual intercourse in an unnatural or unwanted manner, forced sexual intercourse with others for commercial purposes and/or certain purposes. 12. Victim is a woman and child who experiences misery and/or suffering either directly or indirectly as a result of violence. 13. Women in conflict with the law is a woman in conflict with the law, woman as a victim, woman as a witness or woman as a party. 14. Child is a person under 18 years of age, including those in the womb. 15. Family is the smallest unit in society consisting of husband and wife, or husband and wife and their children, or father and children, or mother and children, or blood relatives in direct lineage upward or downward up to the third degree. 16. Parents are biological father and/or mother, or step father and/or mother, or adoptive father and/or mother. 12. Guardian is a person or entity that in reality exercises parental authority as a parent to a child. 18. Neglected child is a child whose needs are not properly met, whether physical, mental, spiritual, or social. 19. Child with Disability is a child who experiences physical and/or mental impairment that disrupts their growth and development normally. 20. Child with excellence is a child who has extraordinary intelligence, or has special potential and/or talent. 21. Adopted child is a child whose rights are transferred from the environment of authority of the family of parents, legal guardian, or other person responsible for the care, education, and raising of the child, into the family environment of adoptive parents based on a court decision or determination. 22. Foster child is a child cared for by a person or institution, to be provided with guidance, maintenance, care, education, and health, because the parents or one of the parents is unable to ensure the child's normal growth and development. 23. Custody is the power of parents to care for, educate, maintain, nurture, protect, and develop the child in accordance with their religion and abilities, talents, and interests. 24. Child's rights are part of human rights that must be guaranteed, protected, and fulfilled by parents, family, community, government, and the state. 25. Protection is any effort aimed at providing a sense of security to victims carried out by family, advocates, social institutions, police, prosecution, courts, or other parties either temporarily or based on court determination. 26. Child protection is all activities to guarantee and protect children and their rights so they can live, grow, develop, and participate optimally in accordance with human dignity, and receive protection from violence and discrimination. 27. Special protection is protection provided to children in emergency situations, children in conflict with the law, children from minority and isolated groups, children who are exploited economically and/or sexually, children who are trafficked, children who are victims of narcotics, alcohol, psychotropic, and other addictive substances (napza) abuse, children victims of kidnapping, sale, trafficking, children victims of violence both physical and/or mental, children with disabilities, and children victims of abuse and neglect. 28. Service is an action carried out as soon as possible to victims when seeing, hearing and knowing that violence against victims will occur, is occurring or has occurred. 29. Victim recovery is all efforts to strengthen victims of domestic violence to be more empowered both physically and psychologically. 30. Implementation of recovery is all actions that include services and assistance to victims of domestic violence. 31. Recovery implementation officer is a health worker, social worker, volunteer companion, and/or spiritual counselor. 32. Companion is a person who has the expertise to accompany victims in providing counseling, therapy and advocacy for strengthening and self-recovery of victims of violence. 33.

states: Any person who traffics, sells, or kidnaps a child for themselves or to be sold, shall be sentenced to imprisonment for a maximum of 15 (fifteen) years and a minimum of 3 (three) years and a fine of at most Rp. 300,000,000,- (three hundred million rupiah) and at least Rp. 60,000,000,- (sixty million rupiah). These three Articles are highly reformative Articles when compared with the provisions in the Criminal Code, which in Articles 281 to 296 regulate provisions, where the heaviest criminal sanction is Article 295 which is 12 years. When compared, the Child Protection Law has been quite severe in establishing criminal and fine sanctions as regulated in Articles 81 to 83. The problem is, even though the Law has established severe sanctions or punishments, there are still Law Enforcement Officials who have not optimally applied them, so there is still a long way to go, between law in book and law in action. In cases as regulated in Articles 81 to 83, Law Officials often conduct investigations and inquiries that are quite heavy and exhausting for child victims of violence, but in prosecutions and judges' verdicts are still light so they do not accord with justice. Violence against women and children also occurs frequently within the household sphere, even though we have had a law for 13 years, namely Law Number 23 of 2004 concerning the Elimination of Domestic Violence (KDRT), but nowadays domestic violence is increasing in number. For the prevention and handling of domestic violence in Musi Rawas Regency, the Office of Women's Empowerment and Child Protection of Musi Rawas Regency has established the Integrated Service Center for the Protection of Women and Children (P2TP2A) of Musi Rawas Regency, based on the Decree of the Regent of Musi Rawas Number 703/KPTS/KPP/2015 concerning the Establishment of the Integrated Service Center for Women's Empowerment and Child Protection (P2TP2A) of Musi Rawas Regency. The Integrated Service Center for Women's Empowerment and Child Protection (P2TP2A) serves as a place for reporting, handling, rehabilitation and reintegration of victims of violence. If there is domestic violence or other violence affecting women and children, it must be reported to the P2TP2A, however the existence of P2TP2A is not yet widely known by the community. Law Number 23 of 2004 concerning the Elimination of Domestic Violence, essentially aims to realize a household that is sakinah, mawadah, and warohmah, this can be read from the objectives of eliminating domestic violence namely: (a) preventing all forms of domestic violence (KDRT); (b) protecting victims of domestic violence, (c) taking action against perpetrators of domestic violence and (d) maintaining the integrity of a harmonious and prosperous household. So that we better understand the prohibition of domestic violence, the important matters of Law Number 23 of 2004 concerning Domestic Violence will be briefly described as follows:

Types of domestic violence, include:

a. physical violence, is an act that results in (1) pain, (2) illness, or (3) serious injury; b. psychological violence, is an act that results in (1) fear, (2) loss of self-confidence, (3) loss of ability to act, (4) feeling of powerlessness, (5) and/or severe psychological suffering to a person; c. sexual violence includes: (1) forced sexual relations committed against a person including a child, residing within the household sphere, (2) forced sexual relations against someone within the household sphere with another person including a child, for commercial purposes and/or certain purposes; d. household neglect, includes (1) neglecting a person including a child within the household sphere, whereas according to the law applicable to them or because of an agreement or arrangement they are obliged to provide livelihood, care, or maintenance to that person or child, (2) causing economic dependence by restricting and/or prohibiting proper work inside or outside the home so that the victim is under the control of that person. The rights of domestic violence victims are to receive:

(1) protection from family, police, prosecution, court, advocate, social institution, or other parties either temporarily or based on a court order; (2) health services according to medical needs; (3) special handling related to victim confidentiality; (4) accompaniment by social workers and legal assistance at every level of the examination process in accordance with the provisions of laws and regulations and

(5) spiritual guidance services. All parties both from government elements, Law Enforcement Officials (APH) and NGOs, have become members of the P2TP2A of Musi Rawas Regency. The obligation to form a Regional Regulation on the Protection of Women and Children Victims of Violence, is synchronized with the provisions of Law Number 23 of 2014 concerning Regional Government. In this Law it is stipulated that the authority to conduct women's empowerment and child protection is delegated to Regional Governments, so it is a very good opportunity for Regional Governments including the Regional Government of Musi Rawas Regency, nowadays to form Regional Regulations with a perspective of gender equality and justice and children's rights. This Regional Regulation on the Protection of Women and Children Victims of Violence, is formed in accordance with the provisions of Law Number 12 of 2011 concerning the Formation of Legislation. The National Objectives of the Unitary State of the Republic of Indonesia, as regulated in the Preamble of the 1945 Constitution in the fourth paragraph, are stated to include: (1) protecting the entire Indonesian nation and all Indonesian bloodshed, (2) promoting general welfare, (3) developing the intellectual life of the nation and (4) participating in implementing world order based on: (a) independence, (b) lasting peace, and (c) social justice. To achieve these objectives, in accordance with the principles of trias politica, there are three State powers, namely executive power for the administration of government, legislative power as the maker of laws and regulations, and judicial power as the implementer of laws and regulations. In Indonesia, these three powers complement each other, for the implementation of a clean and authoritative government, from the national level to the regional level.

The Republic of Indonesia is a State of Law (rechtstaat) and not a State of Power (machtstaat), so that all actions of its citizens, including those in the form of violence, committed by both men and women, are also regulated by law.

The Rights of Women and Children are recognized as Human Rights (HAM), which must be upheld and respected by all parties, but in reality there are still many women and children who become victims of violence. The commitment of the Central Government to protect children and women is reflected in the legislation under it.

Regional Autonomy that has been implemented has strategic value so that each region forms legislation (Regional Regulations), in addition to expressing local wisdom, also to serve as a guideline for Regional Governments to implement the legislation above it (the 1945 Constitution and Laws) to address legal problems and social problems that occur specifically in each region.

This Regional Regulation on the Protection of Women and Children is based on Pancasila and the 1945 Constitution, and refers to Laws that regulate the protection of women and children victims of violence, including Law Number 7 of 1984 concerning Ratification of the Elimination of All Forms of Discrimination against Women, Law Number 39 of 1999 concerning Human Rights, Law Number 23 of 2002 concerning Child Protection as amended by Law Number 35 of 2014 concerning Amendment to Law Number 23 of 2002 concerning Child Protection, Law Number 29 of 2004 concerning Elimination of Domestic Violence, Law Number 21 of 2007 concerning Eradication of the Crime of Human Trafficking, Law Number 11 of 2012 concerning Juvenile Justice System, Law Number 17 of 2016 concerning Stipulation of Government Regulation in Lieu of Law Number 1 of 2016 concerning Second Amendment to Law Number 23 of 2002 concerning Child Protection into Law, and other related Laws, Law Number 8 of 2016 concerning Persons with Disabilities, Regulation of the Supreme Court Number 3 of 2017 concerning Guidelines for Adjudicating Cases of Women Dealing with the Law. The principles of this Regional Regulation are the principles contained in previous legislation, for example the principle of respect for Human Rights and gender equality and justice, is actually already contained in Article 27

of the 1945 Constitution, which essentially is a legal provision concerning gender equality and justice, while reflecting recognition of human rights, because what is referred to as every Citizen certainly consists of men and women, having the same position in the field of law and government.

Also in Article 28 G paragraph (1) of the 1945 Constitution which essentially regulates that every person, of course both men and women, has the right to protection and freedom from fear. Article 28H paragraph (2) which essentially regulates the rights of citizens to receive facilities and special treatment to obtain equality and justice, of course including women and children victims of violence.

Violence whose victims are women and children occurs both within marriage and outside marriage. Article 1

In this Regional Regulation, what is meant by:

1 . Regency is Musi Rawas Regency; 2. Regency Government is the Government of Musi Rawas Regency; 4

3. Regent is the Regent of Musi Rawas. 4. Domestic Violence is any act against a person, particularly women, which results in misery or suffering physically, sexually, psychologically, and/or domestic neglect including threats to commit acts, coercion, or unlawful deprivation of liberty within the household. 5. Elimination of Domestic Violence is a guarantee provided by the state to prevent the occurrence of domestic violence, prosecute perpetrators of domestic violence, and protect victims of domestic violence. 6. Trafficking in Persons is the act of recruitment, transportation, harboring, transfer, relocation, or receipt of a person by means of threat of violence, use of violence, abduction, confinement, fraud, deception, abuse of power or position of vulnerability, debt bondage or giving payments or benefits, so as to obtain the consent of a person having control over another person, whether conducted within a country or between countries, for the purpose of exploitation or resulting in a person being exploited. 7. Victim of Trafficking in Persons is a person who experiences psychological, mental, physical, sexual, economic, and/or social suffering, resulting from the crime of trafficking in persons. 8. Violence is any act that results in or can result in misery or suffering whether physical, sexual, economic, psychological to the victim. 9. Physical violence is any act that causes pain, injury, wounds, or disability to a person's body, miscarriage, unconsciousness and/or causes death. 10. Psychological violence is an act that causes fear, loss of self-confidence, loss of ability to act, feeling of helplessness and/or severe psychological suffering to a person. 11. Sexual violence is an act in the form of sexual harassment, forced sexual intercourse, forced sexual intercourse in an unnatural or unwanted manner, forced sexual intercourse with others for commercial purposes and/or certain purposes. 12. Victim is a woman and child who experiences misery and/or suffering either directly or indirectly as a result of violence. 13. Women in conflict with the law is a woman in conflict with the law, woman as a victim, woman as a witness or woman as a party. 14. Child is a person under 18 years of age, including those in the womb. 15. Family is the smallest unit in society consisting of husband and wife, or husband and wife and their children, or father and children, or mother and children, or blood relatives in direct lineage upward or downward up to the third degree. 16. Parents are biological father and/or mother, or step father and/or mother, or adoptive father and/or mother. 12. Guardian is a person or entity that in reality exercises parental authority as a parent to a child. 18. Neglected child is a child whose needs are not properly met, whether physical, mental, spiritual, or social. 19. Child with Disability is a child who experiences physical and/or mental impairment that disrupts their growth and development normally. 20. Child with excellence is a child who has extraordinary intelligence, or has special potential and/or talent. 21. Adopted child is a child whose rights are transferred from the environment of authority of the family of parents, legal guardian, or other person responsible for the care, education, and raising of the child, into the family environment of adoptive parents based on a court decision or determination. 22. Foster child is a child cared for by a person or institution, to be provided with guidance, maintenance, care, education, and health, because the parents or one of the parents is unable to ensure the child's normal growth and development. 23. Custody is the power of parents to care for, educate, maintain, nurture, protect, and develop the child in accordance with their religion and abilities, talents, and interests. 24. Child's rights are part of human rights that must be guaranteed, protected, and fulfilled by parents, family, community, government, and the state. 25. Protection is any effort aimed at providing a sense of security to victims carried out by family, advocates, social institutions, police, prosecution, courts, or other parties either temporarily or based on court determination. 26. Child protection is all activities to guarantee and protect children and their rights so they can live, grow, develop, and participate optimally in accordance with human dignity, and receive protection from violence and discrimination. 27. Service is an action carried out as soon as possible to victims when seeing, hearing and knowing that violence against victims will occur, is occurring or has occurred. 29. Victim recovery is all efforts to strengthen victims of domestic violence to be more empowered both physically and psychologically. 30. Implementation of recovery is all actions that include services and assistance to victims of domestic violence. 31. Recovery implementation officer is a health worker, social worker, volunteer companion, and/or spiritual counselor. 32. Companion is a person who has the expertise to accompany victims in providing counseling, therapy and advocacy for strengthening and self-recovery of victims of violence. 33.

The National Objectives of the Unitary State of the Republic of Indonesia, as regulated in the Preamble of the 1945 Constitution in the fourth paragraph, are stated to include: (1) protecting the entire Indonesian nation and all Indonesian bloodshed, (2) promoting general welfare, (3) developing the intellectual life of the nation and (4) participating in implementing world order based on: (a) independence, (b) lasting peace, and (c) social justice. To achieve these objectives, in accordance with the principles of trias politica, there are three State powers, namely executive power for the administration of government, legislative power as the maker of laws and regulations, and judicial power as the implementer of laws and regulations. In Indonesia, these three powers complement each other, for the implementation of a clean and authoritative government, from the national level to the regional level.

The Republic of Indonesia is a State of Law (rechtstaat) and not a State of Power (machtstaat), so that all actions of its citizens, including those in the form of violence, committed by both men and women, are also regulated by law.

The Rights of Women and Children are recognized as Human Rights (HAM), which must be upheld and respected by all parties, but in reality there are still many women and children who become victims of violence. The commitment of the Central Government to protect children and women is reflected in the legislation under it.

Regional Autonomy that has been implemented has strategic value so that each region forms legislation (Regional Regulations), in addition to expressing local wisdom, also to serve as a guideline for Regional Governments to implement the legislation above it (the 1945 Constitution and Laws) to address legal problems and social problems that occur specifically in each region.

This Regional Regulation on the Protection of Women and Children is based on Pancasila and the 1945 Constitution, and refers to Laws that regulate the protection of women and children victims of violence, including Law Number 7 of 1984 concerning Ratification of the Elimination of All Forms of Discrimination against Women, Law Number 39 of 1999 concerning Human Rights, Law Number 23 of 2002 concerning Child Protection as amended by Law Number 35 of 2014 concerning Amendment to Law Number 23 of 2002 concerning Child Protection, Law Number 29 of 2004 concerning Elimination of Domestic Violence, Law Number 21 of 2007 concerning Eradication of the Crime of Human Trafficking, Law Number 11 of 2012 concerning Juvenile Justice System, Law Number 17 of 2016 concerning Stipulation of Government Regulation in Lieu of Law Number 1 of 2016 concerning Second Amendment to Law Number 23 of 2002 concerning Child Protection into Law, and other related Laws, Law Number 8 of 2016 concerning Persons with Disabilities, Regulation of the Supreme Court Number 3 of 2017 concerning Guidelines for Adjudicating Cases of Women Dealing with the Law. The principles of this Regional Regulation are the principles contained in previous legislation, for example the principle of respect for Human Rights and gender equality and justice, is actually already contained in Article 27

of the 1945 Constitution, which essentially is a legal provision concerning gender equality and justice, while reflecting recognition of human rights, because what is referred to as every Citizen certainly consists of men and women, having the same position in the field of law and government.

Also in Article 28 G paragraph (1) of the 1945 Constitution which essentially regulates that every person, of course both men and women, has the right to protection and freedom from fear. Article 28H paragraph (2) which essentially regulates the rights of citizens to receive facilities and special treatment to obtain equality and justice, of course including women and children victims of violence.

The National Objectives of the Unitary State of the Republic of Indonesia, as regulated in the Preamble of the 1945 Constitution in the fourth paragraph, are stated to include: (1) protecting the entire Indonesian nation and all Indonesian bloodshed, (2) promoting general welfare, (3) developing the intellectual life of the nation and (4) participating in implementing world order based on: (a) independence, (b) lasting peace, and (c) social justice. To achieve these objectives, in accordance with the principles of trias politica, there are three State powers, namely executive power for the administration of government, legislative power as the maker of laws and regulations, and judicial power as the implementer of laws and regulations. In Indonesia, these three powers complement each other, for the implementation of a clean and authoritative government, from the national level to the regional level.

The Republic of Indonesia is a State of Law (rechtstaat) and not a State of Power (machtstaat), so that all actions of its citizens, including those in the form of violence, committed by both men and women, are also regulated by law.

The Rights of Women and Children are recognized as Human Rights (HAM), which must be upheld and respected by all parties, but in reality there are still many women and children who become victims of violence. The commitment of the Central Government to protect children and women is reflected in the legislation under it.

Regional Autonomy that has been implemented has strategic value so that each region forms legislation (Regional Regulations), in addition to expressing local wisdom, also to serve as a guideline for Regional Governments to implement the legislation above it (the 1945 Constitution and Laws) to address legal problems and social problems that occur specifically in each region.

This Regional Regulation on the Protection of Women and Children is based on Pancasila and the 1945 Constitution, and refers to Laws that regulate the protection of women and children victims of violence, including Law Number 7 of 1984 concerning Ratification of the Elimination of All Forms of Discrimination against Women, Law Number 39 of 1999 concerning Human Rights, Law Number 23 of 2002 concerning Child Protection as amended by Law Number 35 of 2014 concerning Amendment to Law Number 23 of 2002 concerning Child Protection, Law Number 29 of 2004 concerning Elimination of Domestic Violence, Law Number 21 of 2007 concerning Eradication of the Crime of Human Trafficking, Law Number 11 of 2012 concerning Juvenile Justice System, Law Number 17 of 2016 concerning Stipulation of Government Regulation in Lieu of Law Number 1 of 2016 concerning Second Amendment to Law Number 23 of 2002 concerning Child Protection into Law, and other related Laws, Law Number 8 of 2016 concerning Persons with Disabilities, Regulation of the Supreme Court Number 3 of 2017 concerning Guidelines for Adjudicating Cases of Women Dealing with the Law. The National Objectives of the Unitary State of the Republic of Indonesia, as regulated in the Preamble of the 1945 Constitution in the fourth paragraph, are stated to include: (1) protecting the entire Indonesian nation and all Indonesian bloodshed, (2) promoting general welfare, (3) developing the intellectual life of the nation and (4) participating in implementing world order based on: (a) independence, (b) lasting peace, and (c) social justice. To achieve these objectives, in accordance with the principles of trias politica, there are three State powers, namely executive power for the administration of government, legislative power as the maker of laws and regulations, and judicial power as the implementer of laws and regulations. In Indonesia, these three powers complement each other, for the implementation of a clean and authoritative government, from the national level to the regional level.

The Republic of Indonesia is a State of Law (rechtstaat) and not a State of Power (machtstaat), so that all actions of its citizens, including those in the form of violence, committed by both men and women, are also regulated by law.

The Rights of Women and Children are recognized as Human Rights (HAM), which must be upheld and respected by all parties, but in reality there are still many women and children who become victims of violence. The commitment of the Central Government to protect children and women is reflected in the legislation under it.

Regional Autonomy that has been implemented has strategic value so that each region forms legislation (Regional Regulations), in addition to expressing local wisdom, also to serve as a guideline for Regional Governments to implement the legislation above it (the 1945 Constitution and Laws) to address legal problems and social problems that occur specifically in each region.

This Regional Regulation on the Protection of Women and Children is based on Pancasila and the 1945 Constitution, and refers to Laws that regulate the protection of women and children victims of violence, including Law Number 7 of 1984 concerning Ratification of the Elimination of All Forms of Discrimination against Women, Law Number 39 of 1999 concerning Human Rights, Law Number 23 of 2002 concerning Child Protection as amended by Law Number 35 of 2014 concerning Amendment to Law Number 23 of 2002 concerning Child Protection, Law Number 29 of 2004 concerning Elimination of Domestic Violence, Law Number 21 of 2007 concerning Eradication of the Crime of Human Trafficking, Law Number 11 of 2012 concerning Juvenile Justice System, Law Number 17 of 2016 concerning Stipulation of Government Regulation in Lieu of Law Number 1 of 2016 concerning Second Amendment to Law Number 23 of 2002 concerning Child Protection into Law, and other related Laws, Law Number 8 of 2016 concerning Persons with Disabilities, Regulation of the Supreme Court Number 3 of 2017 concerning Guidelines for Adjudicating Cases of Women Dealing with the Law. The National Objectives of the Unitary State of the Republic of Indonesia, as regulated in the Preamble of the 1945 Constitution in the fourth paragraph, are stated to include: (1) protecting the entire Indonesian nation and all Indonesian bloodshed, (2) promoting general welfare, (3) developing the intellectual life of the nation and (4) participating in implementing world order based on: (a) independence, (b) lasting peace, and (c) social justice. To achieve these objectives, in accordance with the principles of trias politica, there are three State powers, namely executive power for the administration of government, legislative power as the maker of laws and regulations, and judicial power as the implementer of laws and regulations. In Indonesia, these three powers complement each other, for the implementation of a clean and authoritative government, from the national level to the regional level.

The Republic of Indonesia is a State of Law (rechtstaat) and not a State of Power (machtstaat), so that all actions of its citizens, including those in the form of violence, committed by both men and women, are also regulated by law.

The Rights of Women and Children are recognized as Human Rights (HAM), which must be upheld and respected by all parties, but in reality there are still many women and children who become victims of violence. The commitment of the Central Government to protect children and women is reflected in the legislation under it.

Regional Autonomy that has been implemented has strategic value so that each region forms legislation (Regional Regulations), in addition to expressing local wisdom, also to serve as a guideline for Regional Governments to implement the legislation above it (the 1945 Constitution and Laws) to address legal problems and social problems that occur specifically in each region.

The National Objectives of the Unitary State of the Republic of Indonesia, as regulated in the Preamble of the 1945 Constitution in the fourth paragraph, are stated to include: (1) protecting the entire Indonesian nation and all Indonesian bloodshed, (2) promoting general welfare, (3) developing the intellectual life of the nation and (4) participating in implementing world order based on: (a) independence, (b) lasting peace, and (c) social justice. To achieve these objectives, in accordance with the principles of trias politica, there are three State powers, namely executive power for the administration of government, legislative power as the maker of laws and regulations, and judicial power as the implementer of laws and regulations. In Indonesia, these three powers complement each other, for the implementation of a clean and authoritative government, from the national level to the regional level.

The Republic of Indonesia is a State of Law (rechtstaat) and not a State of Power (machtstaat), so that all actions of its citizens, including those in the form of violence, committed by both men and women, are also regulated by law.

The Rights of Women and Children are recognized as Human Rights (HAM), which must be upheld and respected by all parties, but in reality there are still many women and children who become victims of violence. The commitment of the Central Government to protect children and women is reflected in the legislation under it.

Regional Autonomy that has been implemented has strategic value so that each region forms legislation (Regional Regulations), in addition to expressing local wisdom, also to serve as a guideline for Regional Governments to implement the legislation above it (the 1945 Constitution and Laws) to address legal problems and social problems that occur specifically in each region.

This Regional Regulation on the Protection of Women and Children is based on Pancasila and the 1945 Constitution, and refers to Laws that regulate the protection of women and children victims of violence, including Law Number 7 of 1984 concerning Ratification of the Elimination of All Forms of Discrimination against Women, Law Number 39 of 1999 concerning Human Rights, Law Number 23 of 2002 concerning Child Protection as amended by Law Number 35 of 2014 concerning Amendment to Law Number 23 of 2002 concerning Child Protection, Law Number 29 of 2004 concerning Elimination of Domestic Violence, Law Number 21 of 2007 concerning Eradication of the Crime of Human Trafficking, Law Number 11 of 2012 concerning Juvenile Justice System, Law Number 17 of 2016 concerning Stipulation of Government Regulation in Lieu of Law Number 1 of 2016 concerning Second Amendment to Law Number 23 of 2002 concerning Child Protection into Law, and other related Laws, Law Number 8 of 2016 concerning Persons with Disabilities, Regulation of the Supreme Court Number 3 of 2017 concerning Guidelines for Adjudicating Cases of Women Dealing with the Law. Article 28H paragraph (2) which essentially regulates the rights of citizens to receive facilities and special treatment to obtain equality and justice, of course including women and children victims of violence.

The National Objectives of the Unitary State of the Republic of Indonesia, as regulated in the Preamble of the 1945 Constitution in the fourth paragraph, are stated to include: (1) protecting the entire Indonesian nation and all Indonesian bloodshed, (2) promoting general welfare, (3) developing the intellectual life of the nation and (4) participating in implementing world order based on: (a) independence, (b) lasting peace, and (c) social justice. To achieve these objectives, in accordance with the principles of trias politica, there are three State powers, namely executive power for the administration of government, legislative power as the maker of laws and regulations, and judicial power as the implementer of laws and regulations. In Indonesia, these three powers complement each other, for the implementation of a clean and authoritative government, from the national level to the regional level.

The Republic of Indonesia is a State of Law (rechtstaat) and not a State of Power (machtstaat), so that all actions of its citizens, including those in the form of violence, committed by both men and women, are also regulated by law.

The Rights of Women and Children are recognized as Human Rights (HAM), which must be upheld and respected by all parties, but in reality there are still many women and children who become victims of violence. The commitment of the Central Government to protect children and women is reflected in the legislation under it.

Regional Autonomy that has been implemented has strategic value so that each region forms legislation (Regional Regulations), in addition to expressing local wisdom, also to serve as a guideline for Regional Governments to implement the legislation above it (the 1945 Constitution and Laws) to address legal problems and social problems that occur specifically in each region.

This Regional Regulation on the Protection of Women and Children is based on Pancasila and the 1945 Constitution, and refers to Laws that regulate the protection of women and children victims of violence, including Law Number 7 of 1984 concerning Ratification of the Elimination of All Forms of Discrimination against Women, Law Number 39 of 1999 concerning Human Rights, Law Number 23 of 2002 concerning Child Protection as amended by Law Number 35 of 2014 concerning Amendment to Law Number 23 of 2002 concerning Child Protection, Law Number 29 of 2004 concerning Elimination of Domestic Violence, Law Number 21 of 2007 concerning Eradication of the Crime of Human Trafficking, Law Number 11 of 2012 concerning Juvenile Justice System, Law Number 17 of 2016 concerning Stipulation of Government Regulation in Lieu of Law Number 1 of 2016 concerning Second Amendment to Law Number 23 of 2002 concerning Child Protection into Law, and other related Laws, Law Number 8 of 2016 concerning Persons with Disabilities, Regulation of the Supreme Court Number 3 of 2017 concerning Guidelines for Adjudicating Cases of Women Dealing with the Law. The principles of this Regional Regulation are the principles contained in previous legislation, for example the principle of respect for Human Rights and gender equality and justice, is actually already contained in Article 27

of the 1945 Constitution, which essentially is a legal provision concerning gender equality and justice, while reflecting recognition of human rights, because what is referred to as every Citizen certainly consists of men and women, having the same position in the field of law and government.

Also in Article 28 G paragraph (1) of the 1945 Constitution which essentially regulates that every person, of course both men and women, has the right to protection and freedom from fear. Article 28H paragraph (2) which essentially regulates the rights of citizens to receive facilities and special treatment to obtain equality and justice, of course including women and children victims of violence.

GENERAL

I.

The National Objectives of the Unitary State of the Republic of Indonesia, as regulated in the Preamble of the 1945 Constitution in the fourth paragraph, are stated to include: (1) protecting the entire Indonesian nation and all Indonesian bloodshed, (2) promoting general welfare, (3) developing the intellectual life of the nation and (4) participating in implementing world order based on: (a) independence, (b) lasting peace, and (c) social justice. To achieve these objectives, in accordance with the principles of trias politica, there are three State powers, namely executive power for the administration of government, legislative power as the maker of laws and regulations, and judicial power as the implementer of laws and regulations. In Indonesia, these three powers complement each other, for the implementation of a clean and authoritative government, from the national level to the regional level.

The Republic of Indonesia is a State of Law (rechtstaat) and not a State of Power (machtstaat), so that all actions of its citizens, including those in the form of violence, committed by both men and women, are also regulated by law.

The Rights of Women and Children are recognized as Human Rights (HAM), which must be upheld and respected by all parties, but in reality there are still many women and children who become victims of violence. The commitment of the Central Government to protect children and women is reflected in the legislation under it.

Regional Autonomy that has been implemented has strategic value so that each region forms legislation (Regional Regulations), in addition to expressing local wisdom, also to serve as a guideline for Regional Governments to implement the legislation above it (the 1945 Constitution and Laws) to address legal problems and social problems that occur specifically in each region.

This Regional Regulation on the Protection of Women and Children is based on Pancasila and the 1945 Constitution, and refers to Laws that regulate the protection of women and children victims of violence, including Law Number 7 of 1984 concerning Ratification of the Elimination of All Forms of Discrimination against Women, Law Number 39 of 1999 concerning Human Rights, Law Number 23 of 2002 concerning Child Protection as amended by Law Number 35 of 2014 concerning Amendment to Law Number 23 of 2002 concerning Child Protection, Law Number 29 of 2004 concerning Elimination of Domestic Violence, Law Number 21 of 2007 concerning Eradication of the Crime of Human Trafficking, Law Number 11 of 2012 concerning Juvenile Justice System, Law Number 17 of 2016 concerning Stipulation of Government Regulation in Lieu of Law Number 1 of 2016 concerning Second Amendment to Law Number 23 of 2002 concerning Child Protection into Law, and other related Laws, Law Number 8 of 2016 concerning Persons with Disabilities, Regulation of the Supreme Court Number 3 of 2017 concerning Guidelines for Adjudicating Cases of Women Dealing with the Law. The principles of this Regional Regulation are the principles contained in previous legislation, for example the principle of respect for Human Rights and gender equality and justice, is actually already contained in Article 27

of the 1945 Constitution, which essentially is a legal provision concerning gender equality and justice, while reflecting recognition of human rights, because what is referred to as every Citizen certainly consists of men and women, having the same position in the field of law and government.

Also in Article 28 G paragraph (1) of the 1945 Constitution which essentially regulates that every person, of course both men and women, has the right to protection and freedom from fear. Article 28H paragraph (2) which essentially regulates the rights of citizens to receive facilities and special treatment to obtain equality and justice, of course including women and children victims of violence.

Violence whose victims are women and children occurs both within marriage and outside marriage. Types of domestic violence, include:

The National Objectives of the Unitary State of the Republic of Indonesia, as regulated in the Preamble of the 1945 Constitution in the fourth paragraph, are stated to include: (1) protecting the entire Indonesian nation and all Indonesian bloodshed, (2) promoting general welfare, (3) developing the intellectual life of the nation and (4) participating in implementing world order based on: (a) independence, (b) lasting peace, and (c) social justice. To achieve these objectives, in accordance with the principles of trias politica, there are three State powers, namely executive power for the administration of government, legislative power as the maker of laws and regulations, and judicial power as the implementer of laws and regulations. In Indonesia, these three powers complement each other, for the implementation of a clean and authoritative government, from the national level to the regional level.

The Republic of Indonesia is a State of Law (rechtstaat) and not a State of Power (machtstaat), so that all actions of its citizens, including those in the form of violence, committed by both men and women, are also regulated by law.

The Rights of Women and Children are recognized as Human Rights (HAM), which must be upheld and respected by all parties, but in reality there are still many women and children who become victims of violence. The commitment of the Central Government to protect children and women is reflected in the legislation under it.

Regional Autonomy that has been implemented has strategic value so that each region forms legislation (Regional Regulations), in addition to expressing local wisdom, also to serve as a guideline for Regional Governments to implement the legislation above it (the 1945 Constitution and Laws) to address legal problems and social problems that occur specifically in each region.

This Regional Regulation on the Protection of Women and Children is based on Pancasila and the 1945 Constitution, and refers to Laws that regulate the protection of women and children victims of violence, including Law Number 7 of 1984 concerning Ratification of the Elimination of All Forms of Discrimination against Women, Law Number 39 of 1999 concerning Human Rights, Law Number 23 of 2002 concerning Child Protection as amended by Law Number 35 of 2014 concerning Amendment to Law Number 23 of 2002 concerning Child Protection, Law Number 29 of 2004 concerning Elimination of Domestic Violence, Law Number 21 of 2007 concerning Eradication of the Crime of Human Trafficking, Law Number 11 of 2012 concerning Juvenile Justice System, Law Number 17 of 2016 concerning Stipulation of Government Regulation in Lieu of Law Number 1 of 2016 concerning Second Amendment to Law Number 23 of 2002 concerning Child Protection into Law, and other related Laws, Law Number 8 of 2016 concerning Persons with Disabilities, Regulation of the Supreme Court Number 3 of 2017 concerning Guidelines for Adjudicating Cases of Women Dealing with the Law. Article 28H paragraph (2) which essentially regulates the rights of citizens to receive facilities and special treatment to obtain equality and justice, of course including women and children victims of violence.

The National Objectives of the Unitary State of the Republic of Indonesia, as regulated in the Preamble of the 1945 Constitution in the fourth paragraph, are stated to include: (1) protecting the entire Indonesian nation and all Indonesian bloodshed, (2) promoting general welfare, (3) developing the intellectual life of the nation and (4) participating in implementing world order based on: (a) independence, (b) lasting peace, and (c) social justice. To achieve these objectives, in accordance with the principles of trias politica, there are three State powers, namely executive power for the administration of government, legislative power as the maker of laws and regulations, and judicial power as the implementer of laws and regulations. In Indonesia, these three powers complement each other, for the implementation of a clean and authoritative government, from the national level to the regional level.

The Republic of Indonesia is a State of Law (rechtstaat) and not a State of Power (machtstaat), so that all actions of its citizens, including those in the form of violence, committed by both men and women, are also regulated by law.

The Rights of Women and Children are recognized as Human Rights (HAM), which must be upheld and respected by all parties, but in reality there are still many women and children who become victims of violence. The commitment of the Central Government to protect children and women is reflected in the legislation under it.

Regional Autonomy that has been implemented has strategic value so that each region forms legislation (Regional Regulations), in addition to expressing local wisdom, also to serve as a guideline for Regional Governments to implement the legislation above it (the 1945 Constitution and Laws) to address legal problems and social problems that occur specifically in each region.

This Regional Regulation on the Protection of Women and Children is based on Pancasila and the 1945 Constitution, and refers to Laws that regulate the protection of women and children victims of violence, including Law Number 7 of 1984 concerning Ratification of the Elimination of All Forms of Discrimination against Women, Law Number 39 of 1999 concerning Human Rights, Law Number 23 of 2002 concerning Child Protection as amended by Law Number 35 of 2014 concerning Amendment to Law Number 23 of 2002 concerning Child Protection, Law Number 29 of 2004 concerning Elimination of Domestic Violence, Law Number 21 of 2007 concerning Eradication of the Crime of Human Trafficking, Law Number 11 of 2012 concerning Juvenile Justice System, Law Number 17 of 2016 concerning Stipulation of Government Regulation in Lieu of Law Number 1 of 2016 concerning Second Amendment to Law Number 23 of 2002 concerning Child Protection into Law, and other related Laws, Law Number 8 of 2016 concerning Persons with Disabilities, Regulation of the Supreme Court Number 3 of 2017 concerning Guidelines for Adjudicating Cases of Women Dealing with the Law. The principles of this Regional Regulation are the principles contained in previous legislation, for example the principle of respect for Human Rights and gender equality and justice, is actually already contained in Article 27

of the 1945 Constitution, which essentially is a legal provision concerning gender equality and justice, while reflecting recognition of human rights, because what is referred to as every Citizen certainly consists of men and women, having the same position in the field of law and government.

Article 28H paragraph (2) which essentially regulates the rights of citizens to receive facilities and special treatment to obtain equality and justice, of course including women and children victims of violence.

The National Objectives of the Unitary State of the Republic of Indonesia, as regulated in the Preamble of the 1945 Constitution in the fourth paragraph, are stated to include: (1) protecting the entire Indonesian nation and all Indonesian bloodshed, (2) promoting general welfare, (3) developing the intellectual life of the nation and (4) participating in implementing world order based on: (a) independence, (b) lasting peace, and (c) social justice. To achieve these objectives, in accordance with the principles of trias politica, there are three State powers, namely executive power for the administration of government, legislative power as the maker of laws and regulations, and judicial power as the implementer of laws and regulations. In Indonesia, these three powers complement each other, for the implementation of a clean and authoritative government, from the national level to the regional level.

The Republic of Indonesia is a State of Law (rechtstaat) and not a State of Power (machtstaat), so that all actions of its citizens, including those in the form of violence, committed by both men and women, are also regulated by law.

The Rights of Women and Children are recognized as Human Rights (HAM), which must be upheld and respected by all parties, but in reality there are still many women and children who become victims of violence. The commitment of the Central Government to protect children and women is reflected in the legislation under it.

Regional Autonomy that has been implemented has strategic value so that each region forms legislation (Regional Regulations), in addition to expressing local wisdom, also to serve as a guideline for Regional Governments to implement the legislation above it (the 1945 Constitution and Laws) to address legal problems and social problems that occur specifically in each region.

This Regional Regulation on the Protection of Women and Children is based on Pancasila and the 1945 Constitution, and refers to Laws that regulate the protection of women and children victims of violence, including Law Number 7 of 1984 concerning Ratification of the Elimination of All Forms of Discrimination against Women, Law Number 39 of 1999 concerning Human Rights, Law Number 23 of 2002 concerning Child Protection as amended by Law Number 35 of 2014 concerning Amendment to Law Number 23 of 2002 concerning Child Protection, Law Number 29 of 2004 concerning Elimination of Domestic Violence, Law Number 21 of 2007 concerning Eradication of the Crime of Human Trafficking, Law Number 11 of 2012 concerning Juvenile Justice System, Law Number 17 of 2016 concerning Stipulation of Government Regulation in Lieu of Law Number 1 of 2016 concerning Second Amendment to Law Number 23 of 2002 concerning Child Protection into Law, and other related Laws, Law Number 8 of 2016 concerning Persons with Disabilities, Regulation of the Supreme Court Number 3 of 2017 concerning Guidelines for Adjudicating Cases of Women Dealing with the Law. The National Objectives of the Unitary State of the Republic of Indonesia, as regulated in the Preamble of the 1945 Constitution in the fourth paragraph, are stated to include: (1) protecting the entire Indonesian nation and all Indonesian bloodshed, (2) promoting general welfare, (3) developing the intellectual life of the nation and (4) participating in implementing world order based on: (a) independence, (b) lasting peace, and (c) social justice. To achieve these objectives, in accordance with the principles of trias politica, there are three State powers, namely executive power for the administration of government, legislative power as the maker of laws and regulations, and judicial power as the implementer of laws and regulations. In Indonesia, these three powers complement each other, for the implementation of a clean and authoritative government, from the national level to the regional level.

The Republic of Indonesia is a State of Law (rechtstaat) and not a State of Power (machtstaat), so that all actions of its citizens, including those in the form of violence, committed by both men and women, are also regulated by law.

The National Objectives of the Unitary State of the Republic of Indonesia, as regulated in the Preamble of the 1945 Constitution in the fourth paragraph, are stated to include: (1) protecting the entire Indonesian nation and all Indonesian bloodshed, (2) promoting general welfare, (3) developing the intellectual life of the nation and (4) participating in implementing world order based on: (a) independence, (b) lasting peace, and (c) social justice. To achieve these objectives, in accordance with the principles of trias politica, there are three State powers, namely executive power for the administration of government, legislative power as the maker of laws and regulations, and judicial power as the implementer of laws and regulations. In Indonesia, these three powers complement each other, for the implementation of a clean and authoritative government, from the national level to the regional level.

The Republic of Indonesia is a State of Law (rechtstaat) and not a State of Power (machtstaat), so that all actions of its citizens, including those in the form of violence, committed by both men and women, are also regulated by law.

The Rights of Women and Children are recognized as Human Rights (HAM), which must be upheld and respected by all parties, but in reality there are still many women and children who become victims of violence. The commitment of the Central Government to protect children and women is reflected in the legislation under it.

Regional Autonomy that has been implemented has strategic value so that each region forms legislation (Regional Regulations), in addition to expressing local wisdom, also to serve as a guideline for Regional Governments to implement the legislation above it (the 1945 Constitution and Laws) to address legal problems and social problems that occur specifically in each region.

1) Article 83

states: Any person who traffics, sells, or kidnaps a child for themselves or to be sold, shall be sentenced to imprisonment for a maximum of 15 (fifteen) years and a minimum of 3 (three) years and a fine of at most Rp. 300,000,000,- (three hundred million rupiah) and at least Rp. 60,000,000,- (sixty million rupiah). These three Articles are highly reformative Articles when compared with the provisions in the Criminal Code, which in Articles 281 to 296 regulate provisions, where the heaviest criminal sanction is Article 295 which is 12 years. When compared, the Child Protection Law has been quite severe in establishing criminal and fine sanctions as regulated in Articles 81 to 83. The problem is, even though the Law has established severe sanctions or punishments, there are still Law Enforcement Officials who have not optimally applied them, so there is still a long way to go, between law in book and law in action. In cases as regulated in Articles 81 to 83, Law Officials often conduct investigations and inquiries that are quite heavy and exhausting for child victims of violence, but in prosecutions and judges' verdicts are still light so they do not accord with justice. Violence against women and children also occurs frequently within the household sphere, even though we have had a law for 13 years, namely Law Number 23 of 2004 concerning the Elimination of Domestic Violence (KDRT), but nowadays domestic violence is increasing in number. For the prevention and handling of domestic violence in Musi Rawas Regency, the Office of Women's Empowerment and Child Protection of Musi Rawas Regency has established the Integrated Service Center for the Protection of Women and Children (P2TP2A) of Musi Rawas Regency, based on the Decree of the Regent of Musi Rawas Number 703/KPTS/KPP/2015 concerning the Establishment of the Integrated Service Center for Women's Empowerment and Child Protection (P2TP2A) of Musi Rawas Regency. The Integrated Service Center for Women's Empowerment and Child Protection (P2TP2A) serves as a place for reporting, handling, rehabilitation and reintegration of victims of violence. If there is domestic violence or other violence affecting women and children, it must be reported to the P2TP2A, however the existence of P2TP2A is not yet widely known by the community. Law Number 23 of 2004 concerning the Elimination of Domestic Violence, essentially aims to realize a household that is sakinah, mawadah, and warohmah, this can be read from the objectives of eliminating domestic violence namely: (a) preventing all forms of domestic violence (KDRT); (b) protecting victims of domestic violence, (c) taking action against perpetrators of domestic violence and (d) maintaining the integrity of a harmonious and prosperous household. So that we better understand the prohibition of domestic violence, the important matters of Law Number 23 of 2004 concerning Domestic Violence will be briefly described as follows:

Types of domestic violence, include:

Child with excellence is a child who has extraordinary intelligence, or has special potential and/or talent. 21. Adopted child is a child whose rights are transferred from the environment of authority of the family of parents, legal guardian, or other person responsible for the care, education, and raising of the child, into the family environment of adoptive parents based on a court decision or determination. 22. Foster child is a child cared for by a person or institution, to be provided with guidance, maintenance, care, education, and health, because the parents or one of the parents is unable to ensure the child's normal growth and development. 23. Custody is the power of parents to care for, educate, maintain, nurture, protect, and develop the child in accordance with their religion and abilities, talents, and interests. 24. Child's rights are part of human rights that must be guaranteed, protected, and fulfilled by parents, family, community, government, and the state. 25. Protection is any effort aimed at providing a sense of security to victims carried out by family, advocates, social institutions, police, prosecution, courts, or other parties either temporarily or based on court determination. 26. Child protection is all activities to guarantee and protect children and their rights so they can live, grow, develop, and participate optimally in accordance with human dignity, and receive protection from violence and discrimination. 27. Special protection is protection provided to children in emergency situations, children in conflict with the law, children from minority and isolated groups, children who are exploited economically and/or sexually, children who are trafficked, children who are victims of narcotics, alcohol, psychotropic, and other addictive substances (napza) abuse, children victims of kidnapping, sale, trafficking, children victims of violence both physical and/or mental, children with disabilities, and children victims of abuse and neglect. 28. Service is an action carried out as soon as possible to victims when seeing, hearing and knowing that violence against victims will occur, is occurring or has occurred. 29. Victim recovery is all efforts to strengthen victims of domestic violence to be more empowered both physically and psychologically. 30. Implementation of recovery is all actions that include services and assistance to victims of domestic violence. 31. Recovery implementation officer is a health worker, social worker, volunteer companion, and/or spiritual counselor. 32. Companion is a person who has the expertise to accompany victims in providing counseling, therapy and advocacy for strengthening and self-recovery of victims of violence. 33.
